items.prompt: What is the name of the force that the weight of air pushes on everything with?

options.label: Gravity
options.feedback: Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward Earth, but the force exerted by the weight of air specifically is called air pressure.

options.label: Friction
options.feedback: Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces, not the force from the weight of air.

options.label: Air pressure
options.feedback: Correct. Air pressure is the force exerted by the weight of the air above, pushing on all surfaces.

options.label: Magnetism
options.feedback: Magnetism is a force from magnets or moving electric charges, unrelated to the weight of air.

items.ok_line: Air pressure comes from the weight of air above pushing down.
items.ko_line: Gravity pulls, but air pressure is the specific force from air's weight.
items.exp_text: Air pressure is the force that the weight of the air above exerts on surfaces. It pushes in all directions because air molecules move and collide with everything.

items.prompt: In which direction does air pressure push on an object?

options.label: Only downward
options.feedback: Air pressure does push downward, but it also pushes sideways and upward because air molecules move in all directions.

options.label: Only upward
options.feedback: Air pressure pushes upward too, but it is not limited to that direction; it acts from every side.

options.label: Only from the sides
options.feedback: Sideways pressure exists, but air pressure also acts from above and below, so it is not only lateral.

options.label: In all directions
options.feedback: Correct. Air molecules bombard surfaces from every side, so air pressure pushes equally in all directions.

items.ok_line: Air pressure acts from above, below, and all sides.
items.ko_line: Air pressure is not only downward, upward, or sideways.
items.exp_text: Air pressure results from countless air molecules hitting a surface. Since molecules move randomly in all directions, the pressure they create acts in every direction at once.

items.prompt: Why does air pressure decrease as you go higher into the atmosphere?

options.label: Because the air gets warmer
options.feedback: Temperature changes with altitude, but the main reason pressure drops is that there is less air above you to press down, not warmth.

options.label: Because there is less air above you
options.feedback: Correct. Higher up, the column of air above you is shorter and less dense, so its weight and the pressure it causes are smaller.

options.label: Because the air becomes pure oxygen
options.feedback: The composition of air stays roughly the same with altitude; it is the amount of air that decreases, not a change to pure oxygen.

options.label: Because gravity weakens with height
options.feedback: Gravity weakens only slightly over the atmosphere's thickness, not enough to explain the large drop in pressure; less air above is the cause.

items.ok_line: Higher up, the weight of air above is smaller.
items.ko_line: Pressure drops due to less air, not due to warmth.
items.exp_text: Air pressure is caused by the weight of the air above. Climbing higher means less air above you, so the pressure on your body decreases.

items.prompt: What happens to air pressure when you go from a mountain top down to sea level?

options.label: It increases
options.feedback: Correct. Descending adds more air above you, so the weight of air and the pressure it exerts become greater.

options.label: It decreases
options.feedback: Pressure decreases when you go up, not down. Going down to sea level puts more air above you, so pressure rises.

options.label: It stays the same
options.feedback: Pressure changes with altitude because the amount of air above changes; it does not stay constant.

options.label: It becomes zero
options.feedback: Pressure never becomes zero at sea level; it is at its greatest there because the full atmosphere is above you.

items.ok_line: Coming down adds more air above, so pressure grows.
items.ko_line: Going down means more air overhead, so pressure rises.
items.exp_text: At sea level, the entire atmosphere sits above you, so the weight of air is maximum and air pressure is highest there.

items.prompt: Why doesn't the air pressure around you crush your body?

options.label: Because air is very light
options.feedback: Air is light, but it still has weight and exerts pressure; the reason you are not crushed is the balance from inside your body, not air's lightness.

options.label: Because air pressure is very weak
options.feedback: Air pressure is actually strong, about 10 newtons per square centimetre at sea level; it does not crush you because pressure inside your body matches it.

options.label: Because your body pushes outward with equal pressure
options.feedback: Correct. The air inside your lungs, ears, and other spaces pushes outward with the same pressure as the air outside, so the forces cancel out.

options.label: Because air pressure only acts on your skin
options.feedback: Air pressure acts on your skin, but your body's internal fluids and gases also press outward, balancing the external pressure.

items.ok_line: Internal air pushes outward equally, so no crushing occurs.
items.ko_line: Air pressure is strong, but inside pressure matches it.
items.exp_text: Your body contains air and fluids that press outward. This outward pressure equals the inward pressure of the atmosphere, so you feel no net force.

items.prompt: What causes the 'pop' in your ears when you change altitude quickly?

options.label: The air inside your ears warming up
options.feedback: Warming air might change pressure slightly, but the pop is about the difference between inside and outside air pressure, not temperature.

options.label: The air pressure inside your ears equalizing with the outside pressure
options.feedback: Correct. When outside pressure changes, the air trapped in your ear has a different pressure; the pop is the small tube opening to let air move and balance it.

options.label: Your eardrum breaking
options.feedback: Your eardrum does not break during normal altitude changes; the pop is the equalization of pressure through the Eustachian tube, not a rupture.

options.label: The air in your ears becoming pure oxygen
options.feedback: The air in your ears stays a mixture like outside air; it is pressure changes, not gas composition changes, that cause the pop.

items.ok_line: The pop is air moving to balance pressures.
items.ko_line: The pop is equalization, not damage to the eardrum.
items.exp_text: A tube connects your middle ear to your throat. When outside pressure changes, this tube opens briefly, letting air flow in or out until the pressure matches outside air pressure.

items.prompt: Which part of the atmosphere has the highest air pressure?

options.label: The stratosphere
options.feedback: The stratosphere is higher up, where there is less air above, so its pressure is lower than at ground level.

options.label: The thermosphere
options.feedback: The thermosphere is very high above Earth, with very little air, so air pressure there is extremely low.

options.label: The exosphere
options.feedback: The exosphere is the outermost layer, where air is extremely thin, so pressure is nearly zero.

options.label: The troposphere, at sea level
options.feedback: Correct. The troposphere is the lowest layer, and at sea level the full weight of the atmosphere above presses down, giving the highest pressure.

items.ok_line: Sea level has the most air above, so highest pressure.
items.ko_line: Higher layers have less air above, so lower pressure.
items.exp_text: Air pressure is greatest where the column of air above is thickest, which is at the bottom of the atmosphere, near sea level in the troposphere.

items.prompt: Why does a balloon expand when you take it from sea level up a high mountain?

options.label: Because the outside air pressure decreases
options.feedback: Correct. The gas inside the balloon still has the same pressure, but with less outside pressure pressing on it, the balloon expands until the inside pressure drops to match.

options.label: Because the air inside the balloon heats up
options.feedback: Heating would expand the balloon, but rising to a mountain typically brings cooler air, not warmer, so that is not the reason.

options.label: Because the balloon's rubber stretches on its own
options.feedback: Rubber does not stretch spontaneously; it is the imbalance between inside and outside pressure that forces it to expand.

options.label: Because there is more air inside the balloon
options.feedback: The amount of air inside the balloon does not change as you climb; only the external pressure changes.

items.ok_line: Lower outside pressure lets the balloon swell.
items.ko_line: Higher altitude is cooler, so heating is not the cause.
items.exp_text: A balloon contains gas at a pressure close to the outside. When outside pressure drops, the inside gas pushes harder relative to outside, so the balloon expands until pressures balance.

items.prompt: What does the 'pressure' in air pressure refer to?

options.label: The temperature of the air
options.feedback: Temperature is a measure of how hot or cold the air is, not the force it exerts on surfaces.

options.label: The speed of the wind
options.feedback: Wind speed is how fast air moves, while air pressure is the force from the weight of air, unrelated to motion.

options.label: The force the air exerts on a surface
options.feedback: Correct. Air pressure is the amount of force air molecules push against a given area of surface.

options.label: The amount of water vapour in the air
options.feedback: Water vapour content is called humidity, not pressure; pressure is about the force from the air's weight.

items.ok_line: Air pressure is the push of air on a surface.
items.ko_line: Pressure is a force, not a measure of heat.
items.exp_text: Air pressure measures how strongly air molecules push against a surface. It results from the weight of the air column above, and it acts on every surface it touches.

items.prompt: Which of these places has the lowest air pressure?

options.label: At sea level
options.feedback: Sea level has the most air above it, so it has the highest pressure, not the lowest.

options.label: At the top of Mount Everest
options.feedback: Correct. High on a mountain, there is much less air above you, so the weight of air and the pressure are very low compared to sea level.

options.label: In a valley between mountains
options.feedback: A valley is lower than mountain tops, so more air lies above it, giving higher pressure than high altitudes.

options.label: On a beach at the coast
options.feedback: A beach is near sea level, so it experiences high air pressure, similar to the sea level value.

items.ok_line: The highest point has the least air above.
items.ko_line: Lower places have more air above, so higher pressure.
items.exp_text: Air pressure depends on the height of the air column above. Mount Everest's top is very high, with a thin air column, so its pressure is far lower than at sea level.
